newsitem.title: FRANCE: Key union takes tough stand on Elf strike talks.
newsitem.headline: Key union takes tough stand on Elf strike talks.

text.p: France's largest trade union said on Wednesday it would refuse to cooperate with pay talks aimed at resolving a week-old strike at Elf Aquitaine as the oil giant tried to unknot problems caused by French refinery shutdowns.
The Socialist-backed CFDT said it would go to talks between unions and employers set for Thursday on pay and working conditions, but only to set out its demands on employment.
These are not part of the talks' agenda, Elf officials said.

The strike over job cuts at Elf's three French oil refineries halted a quarter of the country's refining capacity for a seventh day on Wednesday and workers vowed to keep up their action until at least Thursday.
"The management has replied to our demands with scorn," the CFDT said in a statement.

It said it would continue to campaign against plans to shed 330 jobs or 10 percent of the staff at Elf refining subsidiary Elf Antar France. Elf says the plans are indispensible to future performance and it will only discuss other items such as pay.
Officials at Elf and other oil firms said the closure of its plants was creating a logistical nightmare and raising the cost of keeping petrol stations and other key oil outlets supplied.
Oil traders said Elf had been forced to buy petrol on the European market this week to replace some of the 100,000 barrels (3.5 million U.K. gallons) per day it manufactures in France.
But there were no reports of shortages, with most tanks, ironically, still full following a 12-day blockade by truck drivers which hit oil facilities in a strike ending last week.
An Elf spokesman declined to comment.
Elf strikers made a gesture to the company on Wednesday by offering to allow road deliveries from the stricken plants for several hours on Thursday in exchange for talks.

Production inside the refineries would stay at a standstill, however, union officials said, adding there had been some rows with management about how many people should be left behind on full pay to keep the gas-filled distillation towers safe.
The refineries have combined capacity of about 440,000 barrels per day -- three quarters of Elf's European total.
A flexible French oil industry network which allows rival oil firms to exchange products among themselves may have eased some of Elf's problems, oil traders said.

Unions meanwhile made some progress in efforts to spread the dispute across the oil industry, where labour leaders say 1,700 jobs are threatened in all by plans to slim down and reorganise the French refining industry.
Several unions caused for various actions on December 10.

Unions also agreed to call a 24-hour strike at Shell's refinery at Berre in southern France for Monday, December 9. Protests continued at Elf's Atochem chemicals unit. Unions said they were also talking about possible disruption at Esso France, a unit of U.S. giant Exxon Corp.
